topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to European digital public health contexts and may not fully transfer to Australian health systems, which have different regulatory frameworks, funding models, and organisational structures.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your health workforce by reviewing the framework's capability areas, then map gaps against current training programs.

Use the competency framework as a benchmark to design or audit AI literacy training for public health teams, ensuring coverage of both technical and governance competencies relevant to digital health implementation.

Recognise that European health system contexts differ from Australia's — adapt the framework's recommendations to align with NHMRC guidelines, Australian privacy law, and local health service priorities rather than adopting wholesale.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to EU public health systems — findings may not transfer to Australian healthcare contexts, which have different regulatory frameworks, workforce structures, and digital infrastructure maturity. Results are specific to public health rather than broader organisational settings.
takeaways: Use a structured evidence gap analysis approach to identify which digital literacy competencies your organisation is actually measuring versus which remain unmapped — this can reveal blind spots in your current upskilling assessments.

Applying multiple frameworks (as the study does) helps expose definitional inconsistencies in 'digital literacy' across teams — consider adopting a shared framework in your organisation to ensure consistent baseline expectations before rolling out AI capability development.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case studies and examples may reflect developed economies and larger organisations.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as fundamentally a people challenge, not just a technology implementation—this reframes training priorities from technical tools to workforce readiness and role redesign.
Map which roles will be augmented, transformed, or displaced by AI in your organisation, then design targeted upskilling pathways for each group rather than one-size-fits-all literacy programs.
Establish clear accountability for AI capability development among team leaders and managers, as they are critical influencers of employee engagement with and adoption of AI tools.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on middle school education context; applicability to adult employee AI literacy development in organisational settings would require adaptation.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation—consider structuring your AI upskilling programmes to connect AI concepts to existing digital tools and practices employees already use.

Middle school frameworks emphasise foundational understanding before technical skill-building; apply this principle to adult learners by starting with AI literacy concepts and real-world business applications before advanced technical training.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development contexts. Generalisability to other sectors and geographic regions unclear from snippet. Geographic scope not specified.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured development programs that build confidence and competence — design programs to move staff from skepticism to practical readiness rather than assuming buy-in.

In technical fields like public health, position AI literacy development as essential professional upskilling for educators, not just for students — this frames it as career relevance rather than disruption.

Institutional support for faculty development (time, resources, training design) is a prerequisite for organisational AI literacy; bottom-up individual learning efforts are insufficient without systemic backing.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a discourse-based review likely covering international examples, but without specified geographic scope or systematic methodology, applicability may vary by healthcare context and AI maturity in different regions.
takeaways: Identify specific AI pitfalls in your healthcare or care setting (e.g., algorithmic bias, loss of human connection, data privacy risks) before implementation to design mitigating safeguards that preserve person-centred values.

Develop a framework that embeds person-centred care principles into AI system design and deployment, ensuring AI augments rather than replaces human judgment and relationship-building in care interactions.
Establish clear protocols for staff training on both AI capabilities and limitations so teams can use AI tools appropriately without over-relying on them or compromising care quality.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which cannot be determined from the title and snippet alone. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) is likely applicable across sectors, but specific findings may be limited by the study's geographic scope and participant demographics.
takeaways: Generative AI can either replace or enhance employee knowledge work depending on implementation approach — clarifying whether AI is positioned as a tool for augmentation (supporting existing skills) versus automation (replacing tasks) may be critical for preserving engagement and knowledge-building behaviors.

Monitor for the 'deskilling paradox': over-reliance on generative AI for routine knowledge tasks may reduce employees' opportunities to develop deeper expertise, even as productivity increases in the short term.
Design AI integration explicitly around knowledge-sharing and collaborative learning rather than task displacement to maintain employees' cognitive engagement with their work.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from title and snippet alone — context on sample size, geography, and sector would be needed to assess generalisability. The focus on 'paternalistic leadership' may be more culturally relevant in Asia-Pacific contexts where this leadership style is more prevalent.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in how AI is implemented and customised for their roles — this sense of 'ownership' may increase willingness to collaborate with and adopt AI systems.

Under paternalistic leadership, create space for 'AI crafting' (i.e., allowing employees to shape how they work with AI) as a mechanism to strengthen both psychological ownership and collaborative intent with AI systems.

Consider whether your organisation's leadership style (particularly how directive vs. participative it is) affects how employees respond to AI adoption initiatives — paternalistic contexts may require different engagement strategies than other leadership models.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings; labour market conditions, employment trends, and psychological impacts may differ in Australia due to different industrial relations frameworks, award wages, and economic conditions.
takeaways: Acknowledge and name uncertainty in your workplace conversations with employees — unspoken anxiety about AI disruption and job security can amplify psychological distress; explicit communication about organisational strategy reduces rumination.

Design transition support programmes that address both capability gaps and emotional responses to change — practical reskilling initiatives are more effective when paired with psychological safety and access to employee assistance resources.

Monitor team wellbeing indicators (engagement, retention, sickness absence) during periods of AI implementation, as uncertainty about future roles can trigger disengagement even before formal job changes occur.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — opinion piece without empirical data or specific organisational context. Observations likely reflect general workplace trends in knowledge-work environments but lack rigorous evidence base.
takeaways: Monitor and create guidelines for employees' use of generative AI tools for personal workplace support (e.g., emotional processing, decision-making) to mitigate risks around data privacy, accuracy, and over-reliance on AI rather than human connection.

Strengthen manager and peer support channels so employees feel they have safe human alternatives for personal and professional challenges, reducing the appeal of turning to AI for sensitive workplace concerns.

Educate teams on AI limitations in providing genuine personal support — lack of contextual understanding, potential biases, and inability to replace human empathy — particularly for high-stakes or emotionally complex situations.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — without access to the full article, the generalisability depends on the study design, sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Address role ambiguity explicitly when introducing generative AI tools — clarify how AI complements vs. replaces employee responsibilities to reduce confusion and friction in adoption.
Build employee self-efficacy through targeted training and early wins with AI tools — stronger confidence in using AI appears linked to more effective human-AI collaboration.
Recognise that role clarity and personal confidence operate as distinct levers in AI adoption; organisations may need to target both simultaneously rather than assuming one will drive the other.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and medical AI adoption. Generalisability to other healthcare professions or non-healthcare sectors with AI implementation is unclear without access to full methodology.
takeaways: Autonomy is a critical mechanism: supporting staff autonomy when introducing AI tools (rather than using AI to increase control) appears essential for protecting wellbeing during technological change.
Readiness matters before implementation: assess and build AI readiness among clinical staff before deployment to improve both adoption outcomes and staff wellbeing.
Monitor wellbeing longitudinally: track wellbeing across multiple timepoints during AI adoption to catch negative impacts early and adjust implementation approaches.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are based on client work but specific geographic scope, sample sizes, and sectors are not detailed in the snippet. Findings likely most applicable to large organisations with resources for structured change programmes.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' framing (compliance-based) to 'adaptation' framing (capability-building) to foster sustainable behaviour change around AI — this reframes the goal from rollout speed to sustained competence and confidence.
Design change programmes that explicitly target human behaviours and mindsets needed for AI use, rather than treating behaviour change as a secondary outcome of technology deployment.
Consider a phased approach that builds adaptive capacity incrementally, allowing employees time to develop new ways of working rather than expecting immediate proficiency.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings may reflect US-centric business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts or other sectors.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and workflows in your organisation where AI adoption could meaningfully reduce routine tasks — use this as a starting point for targeted upskilling rather than organisation-wide rollouts.

Create clear communication about how AI will change job roles, rather than allowing uncertainty to drive resistance — transparency about transition timelines and retraining support increases employee buy-in for behaviour change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case studies and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may reflect biases toward larger organisations that can afford transformation consulting.
takeaways: Design workforce transformation and AI adoption as integrated initiatives, not separate projects — align skills development, role redesign, and change management from the outset rather than deploying AI tools first and reskilling later.

Identify and address workforce mindset barriers early — resistance often stems from job security fears and skill gaps; transparent communication about role evolution and structured upskilling pathways reduce adoption friction.

Map current capability gaps against future AI-enabled roles to prioritise targeted development — avoid generic AI literacy training in favour of role-specific competencies that employees can immediately apply.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full text — likely limited by sample characteristics and organisational context, though the theoretical framework (approach-avoidance motivation) may apply across settings.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger two opposing employee responses: approach-motivated job crafting (seeking new tasks, skill development) vs. avoidance-motivated crafting (task reduction, withdrawal) — understanding which employees tend toward which response helps target support.

Organisations can influence the direction of job crafting by framing AI as a tool for enhancing roles rather than replacing workers, and by providing clear pathways for reskilling to activate approach motivation in your workforce.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to Chinese primary and secondary school teachers and may not generalise to other cultural contexts, educational systems, or sectors. Chinese education policy, institutional pressures, and teacher training systems differ substantially from Australia's.
takeaways: AI adoption in teaching creates a 'double-edged sword' — while it can enable innovative teaching practices, it simultaneously creates threat responses (anxiety, resistance) in some teachers; behaviour change initiatives must address both the opportunity and the psychological barriers simultaneously rather than assuming adoption automatically drives innovation.

The effect of AI on teaching behaviour is mediated by how teachers perceive the change — framing AI as a 'challenge' to overcome (growth mindset) versus a 'threat' to job security produces opposite behavioural outcomes; leaders should deliberately shape the narrative around AI adoption to emphasise learning and capability-building rather than replacement.

Context matters significantly — Chinese institutional and cultural factors shaped these results; before applying these insights in Australian schools, pilot-test whether teachers here show similar threat-vs-challenge responses, and adapt your change communication strategy accordingly.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global client work and trends, but specific case examples and recommendations may reflect practices in large multinational organisations and may not directly translate to smaller or non-corporate settings.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a standalone training programme — this positions it as strategically important and links it to business outcomes, increasing stakeholder buy-in and resource allocation.

Design AI upskilling interventions that address both technical capability gaps and the psychological/cultural barriers to adoption, as technical training alone will not drive sustained behaviour change across the workforce.

Establish clear accountability structures and incentives for managers to sponsor and reinforce AI capability development in their teams, since frontline adoption depends on leader modelling and reinforcement rather than one-off training events.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New study reveals an unexpected difference between casual and compulsive pornography viewers - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New study reveals an unexpected difference between casual and compulsive pornography viewers  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — would depend on sample size, participant demographics, and whether findings replicate across different populations.
takeaways: The study identifies a measurable behavioural or neurological distinction between occasional and compulsive viewers — suggesting 'compulsive' is not just a matter of frequency, but involves a different underlying mechanism.
This challenges the assumption that pornography consumption exists on a simple spectrum from light to heavy use, implying qualitatively different patterns may be at play.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and demographics, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. The findings likely apply to memory encoding processes broadly, but specific limitations cannot be assessed without full methodology.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising or unexpected moments differently — some personalities may naturally encode shocking events more vividly than others.
Your personality type might explain why you remember some surprising moments crystal-clear while a friend who witnessed the same event has only a fuzzy recollection.
This challenges the assumption that 'surprising' events are equally memorable for everyone — individual differences matter as much as the surprise itself.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline claims of 'shocking differences' are often overstated in science reporting. Actual neuroimaging studies typically involve small, clinical samples and findings don't necessarily translate to population-level understanding of psychopathy.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies on psychopathy are prone to sensationalised headlines — the actual differences are usually more subtle and context-dependent than 'shocking' implies.
Neurobiological variation exists across the psychopathy spectrum, but brain scans alone can't predict behaviour or diagnose personality traits reliably in individuals.
It's a reminder that fascinating neuroscience findings often get compressed into clickable headlines that oversimplify what the research actually shows.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single AI analysis of wine reviews; no information on sample size, review sources, or methodology provided in snippet. Findings may not generalise beyond the specific dataset and language analysed.
takeaways: Wine review language appears to reveal personality traits — a clever demonstration that people's writing style about everyday preferences can inadvertently expose deeper psychological patterns.

This playful intersection of AI text analysis and personality psychology shows how machine learning can uncover hidden connections in seemingly mundane human behaviour that traditional psychology might miss.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to be a cross-cultural study examining personality and music preferences across multiple countries, suggesting broad applicability across diverse populations.
takeaways: Your taste in music tells a consistent story about your personality type worldwide — suggesting personality-to-music links are universal human traits, not culturally constructed.

This challenges the idea that musical preferences are purely shaped by local culture or upbringing; there's a deeper, personality-driven logic to why people around the world gravitate toward similar genres.
It's a fun reminder that despite vast cultural differences, strangers on opposite sides of the globe might bond instantly over their Spotify playlists because they share the same personality wiring.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without full article content — twin study methodology typically allows strong causal inference about genetic vs environmental contributions, but generalisability depends on the specific sample characteristics and population studied.
takeaways: Twin studies can separate nature from nurture in political beliefs — suggesting authoritarianism isn't just learned ideology but has detectable genetic roots.
The finding is counterintuitive because political beliefs feel entirely reasoned and chosen, yet heritable traits appear to predispose people toward authoritarian worldviews.
This kind of research fascinates because it reveals why people with similar upbringings can diverge politically, and why some families cluster around similar political values across generations.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by lack of detail in snippet — unable to assess sample size, geographic scope, or sector coverage. Full article review needed to evaluate applicability to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key lever for helping employees innovate with AI tools rather than resist them — consider assessing and building these capacities in your team.
Frame AI as a job resource rather than a threat to psychological safety; employees with higher psychological capital are more likely to view it as enabling rather than replacing their work.
Invest in resilience and optimism-building interventions alongside AI upskilling to unlock the innovation potential of algorithm-driven work environments.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC surveys typically cover multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition, response rates, and demographic representation would need verification from the full report to assess potential biases.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce fears are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing employee sentiment data against PwC's global benchmarks — this can pinpoint psychological safety gaps requiring targeted intervention.

Use survey findings on workforce hopes (e.g., around autonomy, fairness, or career development) to design or refine team practices that reinforce psychological safety, since unmet hopes often correlate with reduced willingness to speak up or take interpersonal risks.

Consider whether geographic or sectoral differences in the PwC data apply to your Australian workforce — global trends may not reflect local labour market conditions, regulations, or cultural norms affecting how psychological safety manifests.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on academic teams in multicultural settings; generalisability to broader organisational contexts and non-academic sectors unclear without full article access.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to support inclusive leadership practices that actively address gendered dynamics in multicultural teams — consider how your organisation might audit or implement AI-assisted approaches to reduce unconscious bias in team composition and decision-making.

Psychological safety for underrepresented groups (particularly women in academic contexts) may require deliberate integration of inclusive leadership principles into AI systems, not just passive algorithmic design — evaluate whether your current AI implementations actively promote equity or risk reinforcing existing disparities.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, industry sectors, and geographic scope, which are not detailed in the provided information.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively affect employee mental health if it erodes psychological safety; leaders should explicitly prioritise creating safe spaces for questions and concerns about AI implementation to mitigate depression and anxiety.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor during AI transitions — ensure your organisation models transparent decision-making about AI use, solicits employee input on implementation, and addresses fairness concerns openly rather than imposing systems unilaterally.

Monitor psychological safety metrics (e.g. willingness to speak up, trust in leadership) before, during, and after AI rollouts as early warning indicators of employee distress; low scores signal the need for intervention.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on global consulting experience and client data, but specific sample composition, size, and geographic distribution are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that encourage speaking up across hierarchy levels — psychological safety works as an equaliser when leaders visibly solicit input from junior staff and respond non-defensively to dissent.

Audit whose voices are heard in meetings and decision-making; psychological safety has differential impact if some groups (e.g. minorities, women, introverts) remain silent despite formal permission to speak.
Measure psychological safety alongside engagement and innovation metrics to track whether safety initiatives are actually reducing status-based silencing in your organisation.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — practitioner guidance from a US HR professional body; principles are broadly applicable but may reflect US workplace norms and HR practices.
takeaways: Identify the four specific leadership behaviours that build psychological safety according to SHRM, and audit which ones your leadership team already models consistently vs. where gaps exist.
Use the article's framework to design one targeted intervention (e.g., structured listening in meetings, transparent error handling) that addresses the largest psychological safety gap in your team.

Create accountability by asking leaders to describe a recent moment they encouraged dissent or admitted uncertainty — this surfaces whether the espoused principles are actually embedded in daily practice.
